title: Email Business Activities Extraction and Annotation
abstract: Treats professional email as a source for recovering undocumented business activities and associated metadata useful for business-process analysis. The work is directly relevant to activity-centric structuring of workplace email, while not establishing the complete structured action benchmark required by the target gaps.

admission.reason: The topic is authentic professional email and business-activity recovery, but the abstract describes business-process activity discovery and associated metadata rather than extraction of work requests, assignments, owners, deadlines, conditions, or decision arguments. Topic words match F1, but the demonstrated capability does not establish action-item extraction at the semantic granularity required here.

title: Annotations for Power Relations on Email Threads
abstract: Annotates Enron email threads for organizational and situational power, influence, communication control, and utterance-level displays of power. It does not extract assignees, but it provides direct authentic-email evidence for organizational context that could be relevant when responsibility is implicit rather than named locally.
venue: Proceedings of the Eighth International Conference on Language Resources and Evaluation (LREC 2012)

admission.reason: The Enron annotations establish organizational power and influence context, not assignee or responsible-party extraction. Organizational context could later be an input to owner inference, but the abstract does not show recovery of implicit owners or any action arguments, so it does not materially strengthen F6 or close gap-3.

title: On the Elicitation and Annotation of Business Activities Based on Emails
abstract: Studies discovery and annotation of business-process activities from email and extracts associated metadata such as participant roles, attachment types, and link domains. It provides direct evidence that authentic email can be structured around business activities, but the activity metadata is not equivalent to a fully annotated action-item owner/deadline/condition representation.

admission.reason: The abstract concerns elicitation of business-process activities and metadata such as participant roles, attachment types, and link domains. Those metadata are not shown to be semantic action arguments such as requester, assignee, action object, deadline, or condition. It is adjacent to F1 but does not demonstrate the required capability.

title: Building A Corporate Corpus For Threads Constitution
abstract: Describes construction and privacy-preserving processing of a corpus of real corporate email intended for conversation-thread reconstruction and analysis. The corpus is relevant to authentic workplace email and contextual reconstruction, including discussion of information such as commitments and deadlines, but it does not itself establish a structured action or decision extraction benchmark.
venue: Proceedings of the Student Research Workshop Associated with RANLP 2021

admission.reason: This is primarily a real-corporate-email corpus construction and thread-reconstruction paper. Mentioning commitments or deadlines as potentially useful information is not equivalent to annotating or extracting them. It therefore does not materially strengthen F13 or F14 for the act/action representations required in this round.

title: Automatic Decision Detection in Meeting Speech
abstract: Develops automatic detection of decision-related dialogue acts and decision segments in complete meeting transcripts. It provides transfer evidence for modeling decision discourse but does not establish structured decision extraction from email or enterprise chat.

admission.reason: The abstract demonstrates meeting decision-act and decision-segment detection, but that capability is substantially covered by the admitted meeting-domain papers manual-90280d2776 and 1606.07849, which add distinctions between proposal/agreement roles or explicit decision-cue-to-content relations. Reading this additional generic decision detector is unlikely to materially strengthen F5.

title: Evaluating the Quality of AI-Generated Resolutions from Conversational vs Structured Sources: Implications for Enterprise Knowledge Automation
abstract: Evaluates extraction of IT-support resolutions from noisy enterprise Slack and Microsoft Teams conversations against resolutions derived from structured ticket sources. This supplies empirical evidence about structured knowledge extraction from authentic enterprise chat, but its resolution representation does not directly close the action-owner, deadline-binding, or condition-attachment gaps.
venue: NeurIPS 2025 Workshop: Reliable ML from Unreliable Data

admission.reason: The paper extracts IT-support resolutions from Slack and Microsoft Teams and compares them with structured-ticket resolutions, but the target representation is a support resolution rather than a request, commitment, assignment, approval, rejection, owner-deadline structure, or condition-attached action. It is authentic enterprise-chat evidence, but the capability is outside the core semantic extraction streams for this round.

title: TAGPRIME: A Unified Framework for Relational Structure Extraction
abstract: Presents a unified conditional sequence-tagging framework for relational structure extraction, including event arguments conditioned on triggers and role-related information. It is transfer evidence for extracting structured trigger-argument spans but is not an authentic workplace email/chat benchmark.
venue: Proceedings of the 61st Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers)

admission.reason: TAGPRIME is a strong generic relational-structure extraction framework, but the abstract does not specifically address implicit workplace owners, deadline binding, condition attachment, or workplace acts. Its trigger-conditioned argument extraction substantially overlaps the generic structured-span capability supplied here by the admitted DyGIE++ paper, which additionally emphasizes contextualized spans and cross-sentence information. The VERIFIED identity does not outweigh that redundancy.

title: Learning with Structured Representations for Negation Scope Extraction
abstract: Models negation-scope extraction with structured representations rather than independent token decisions. This is transfer evidence for scope attachment and span extraction, not direct evidence for negated workplace requests or obligations.
venue: Proceedings of the 56th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Short Papers

admission.reason: The paper is relevant to F10, but its contribution is specifically structured negation-scope extraction and is substantially redundant for this reading round with the admitted 2016 speculation-and-negation scope paper, which covers both negation and uncertainty-like speculation. The abstract does not add workplace action attachment or condition/exception handling sufficient to justify another slot.

title: What Decisions Have You Made?: Automatic Decision Detection in Meeting Conversations
abstract: Studies automatic detection of decision-making dialogue acts and decision-related segments in multi-party meeting conversations using lexical, prosodic, contextual, and topical information. This is transfer evidence from meetings rather than asynchronous workplace email or enterprise chat.
venue: Human Language Technologies 2007: The Conference of the North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics

admission.reason: This meeting-domain paper demonstrates decision-act and decision-segment detection, but its capability is duplicated by stronger admitted F5 candidates in this set, especially manual-90280d2776 for proposal/agreement structure and 1606.07849 for relating decision cues to decision content. It does not add structured arguments needed by the open gaps.

title: Can Prosody Aid the Automatic Classification of Dialog Acts in Conversational Speech?
abstract: Investigates automatic dialogue-act classification in conversational speech and the contribution of prosodic information alongside other evidence. It is foundational transfer literature from the 1990s rather than direct workplace email extraction evidence.

admission.reason: The paper studies generic conversational-speech dialogue-act classification and prosody. It is historically relevant but neither workplace-specific nor focused on the request, commitment, decision, owner, deadline, or condition distinctions needed here. The capability is too remote from the current gaps to justify a reading slot.

title: Meeting Decision Tracker: Making Meeting Minutes with De-Contextualized Utterances
abstract: Presents a system that detects decision utterances in meetings and rewrites them into de-contextualized decision items for minutes. It is transfer evidence for decision detection, but generated de-contextualization is weaker evidence for exact source-span and structured-argument extraction.
venue: Proceedings of the 2nd Conference of the Asia-Pacific Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics and the 12th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing: System Demonstrations

admission.reason: The system detects meeting decisions and rewrites them into de-contextualized minutes, but generated de-contextualization is not evidence for exact source-span preservation or structured decision arguments. Decision detection itself is already better represented by admitted F5 papers, so this system demonstration does not materially strengthen the stream.

title: Tracing Linguistic Markers of Influence in a Large Online Organisation
abstract: Studies linguistic markers of influence in a large collaborative standards organization using a long-running IETF email archive containing organizational interactions. It does not perform action-owner extraction, but it is direct workplace-like email evidence that organizational and conversational context carries information about participant roles and influence.
venue: Proceedings of the 61st Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 2: Short Papers)

admission.reason: The IETF email domain is directly relevant organizational communication, but the paper studies linguistic markers of influence rather than action ownership, assignment, addressee resolution, requests, commitments, or decisions. Organizational role signals might become auxiliary features, but the abstract does not demonstrate the target extraction capability.

title: CORE - an LLM-Powered System for Resolution Mining and Retrieval from Conversational Platforms
abstract: Presents an LLM-based system that mines and structures support resolutions from enterprise conversational platforms including Slack and Microsoft Teams and makes them retrievable. It is direct enterprise-chat extraction evidence, but resolution mining is not itself a benchmark for action owner, deadline, conditionality, or decision arguments.
venue: 2026 IEEE 42nd International Conference on Data Engineering Workshops

admission.reason: CORE provides current direct evidence that enterprise Slack and Teams conversations can be mined into structured support resolutions, but the abstract does not show extraction of action owners, deadlines, conditions, requests, commitments, approvals, rejections, or decision arguments. Resolution mining is adjacent but not a demonstrated solution to any open academic gap in this round.

title: Improving Implicit Semantic Role Labeling by Predicting Semantic Frame Arguments
abstract: Improves implicit semantic-role labeling by modeling expected semantic-frame arguments and recovering roles that are not overtly expressed near a predicate. This is linguistic transfer evidence for implicit argument recovery rather than direct workplace assignee extraction.
venue: Proceedings of the Eighth International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing

admission.reason: The paper is relevant to implicit semantic roles, but the admitted manual-69bc2555ab directly addresses binding implicit roles to non-local discourse entities and the admitted 2020 implicit-event-argument paper adds document-level span recovery. This candidate's expected-frame-argument modeling is useful but substantially redundant for the present F11 reading objective.

title: Dialogue Act Modeling for Automatic Tagging and Recognition of Conversational Speech
abstract: Develops statistical dialogue-act modeling and automatic tagging for conversational speech using lexical, discourse-sequence, and prosodic information. It is foundational computational evidence for contextual speech-act classification and helps establish the pre-transformer lineage behind later email and workplace-dialogue act work.

admission.reason: This is foundational generic dialogue-act modeling for conversational speech. Although it demonstrates use of discourse sequence context, it does not focus on workplace requests, commitments, decisions, assignments, or argument extraction and is superseded for this round by candidates with direct organizational-email acts or more targeted meeting decision structures.
